title: one-to-one correspondence and many-to-one correspondence, using bar graphs and pictographs

lesson.title: One Picture, Many Things: Reading Pictographs and Bar Graphs

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Last week our school had a bottle-and-can recycling drive. Division One brought in twenty cans, Division Two brought thirty-five, Division Three brought fifteen, and Division Four brought forty. Now we want to make a poster with little can pictures on it. Uh oh — if we draw one picture for every single can, we would have to draw one hundred and ten tiny cans! That would take all afternoon and it would look like a big messy pile.

Let's look at what we were doing first. Drawing one picture for one can is called one-to-one correspondence. One picture stands for exactly one thing. Here are five little dots for five cans. It's easy to understand, and it's perfect when the numbers are small — but with one hundred and ten cans, our marker would run out!

So here is the clever trick. What if one picture stands for a whole group of five cans? That's called many-to-one correspondence — many things, shown by one symbol. Look at these four groups of five dots. That's four times five, which is twenty cans, and we only had to draw four pictures. Four pictures instead of twenty. Much faster!

visual.caption: Many-to-one: each picture stands for 5 cans

steps.say: The most important part of any pictograph is the key. The key is the little note at the bottom that says what one symbol is worth. Ours says: one can picture equals five cans. Once you know the key, you can count up like skip counting. One picture is five cans, two pictures is ten, three pictures is fifteen, four pictures is twenty. See how the bottom row jumps by five each time?

visual.caption: Key: 1 picture = 5 cans (skip count by five)

steps.say: Now let's build our real pictograph together. Division One had twenty cans, and twenty divided by five is four, so we draw four pictures. Division Two had thirty-five cans, and thirty-five divided by five is seven pictures. Division Three had fifteen cans, that's three pictures. Division Four had forty cans, that's eight pictures. Look at the top row of pictures and the bottom row of cans — the pictures are small numbers, but they tell us the big numbers.

visual.caption: Pictures drawn vs. cans they stand for

steps.say: Bar graphs do the very same trick, but with squares instead of pictures. On this bar graph, each little square going up the side is worth five cans, not one. So when I want to read Division Two's bar, I count the squares — one, two, three, four, five, six, seven — and then I multiply. Seven squares times five cans each is thirty-five cans. Division Four's bar is eight squares tall, and eight times five is forty cans. Count the squares, then multiply by what one square is worth.

visual.caption: Each square on the scale = 5 cans

steps.say: Here's a slightly trickier one from our bake sale. On this pictograph, one coin picture stands for ten dollars. The Grade Four row has four whole coins and one half coin. Four whole coins is four times ten, which is forty dollars, and the half coin is half of ten, which is five dollars. So forty plus five is forty-five dollars. The Grade Five row has three whole coins, so that's three times ten, or thirty dollars. Half a symbol just means half of what the key says!

visual.caption: Money raised in dollars (1 coin picture = $10)

steps.say: So remember: always find the key first. It tells you whether one symbol means one thing, or a whole group of things. Then count your symbols and multiply. You've got this!

lesson.answer: Read the key first: count the symbols, then multiply by what one symbol is worth — 7 pictures × 5 cans = 35 cans.

practice.question: At the Saturday farmers market in Vancouver, a pictograph shows blueberry baskets sold. The key says one basket picture stands for 5 baskets. Saturday's row has 9 basket pictures. How many baskets were sold on Saturday? And if Sunday sold 30 baskets, how many pictures would Sunday's row need?
